lesson.title: The Active Site: Where an Enzyme's Chemistry Actually Happens
lesson.summary: The active site is a precisely shaped pocket on an enzyme, assembled by tertiary folding, where substrate binds and the actual chemical transformation is carried out by a small set of strategically positioned amino acid side chains.
lesson.body:
The active site of an enzyme is the specific region, usually a cleft, groove, or pocket on the enzyme's surface, where the substrate binds and the catalyzed reaction takes place. Although an enzyme may be built from a chain of hundreds of amino acids, only a small handful of residues, often fewer than ten, actually participate directly in binding the substrate and performing catalysis. The rest of the protein serves mainly as scaffolding, holding those key residues in exactly the right three dimensional arrangement.

That arrangement only exists because of tertiary structure. A polypeptide chain folds so that amino acids scattered widely across the primary sequence, sometimes at opposite ends of the chain, are brought into close physical proximity. It is entirely normal for an active site to be built from residue twelve, residue eighty seven, and residue two hundred and three of the same chain, positioned right next to each other in the folded, three dimensional protein even though they are far apart on paper. Hydrophobic packing, hydrogen bonding, ionic interactions, and the overall geometry of the fold all cooperate to lock these residues into place, forming a pocket with a very particular size, shape, and chemical character.

The chemical character of the active site is just as important as its physical shape. Depending on which amino acid side chains line the pocket, an active site can be strongly polar or largely nonpolar, positively or negatively charged, or capable of forming specific hydrogen bonds in specific orientations. This chemical complementarity between active site and substrate is a major source of an enzyme's specificity: a substrate that fits the geometry but has the wrong charge distribution, or vice versa, generally will not bind well or will not be positioned correctly for catalysis even if it does bind.

Many active sites contain what are called catalytic residues, side chains that do more than just hold the substrate in place. They participate directly in the chemistry, for instance by donating or accepting protons, forming a temporary covalent bond with the substrate, or stabilizing a charged intermediate. A well studied example is the family of serine proteases, enzymes such as chymotrypsin that cleave peptide bonds using a catalytic triad of three residues, serine, histidine, and aspartate, arranged in the active site so that histidine increases the reactivity of serine's hydroxyl group, which then attacks the peptide bond of the substrate.

Understanding the active site as a purpose built structure, assembled by tertiary folding and populated with a small set of functionally critical residues, sets up the next ideas directly. Once a substrate encounters and binds this pocket, it forms what is called an enzyme substrate complex, and the specific fit between substrate and active site, along with the flexibility of that fit, becomes central to explaining both how catalysis proceeds and how the active site can adjust its shape during binding, which is the subject of the induced fit model covered later in this sequence.
